content:
Deadline only 11 days away, sales information just received—simply no time to consider carefully

Ms. Au's family lives in Wang Hoi Court, residing with her husband, three sons and one domestic helper. She is one of the few residents who have not returned the acquisition意向書 by 31 August. Mrs Au said she understands and knows that inevitably she will have to sell the title in the future, but felt that before 31 August, both physically and mentally she was not ready to make this decision.

As a mother of three, her family is her top priority—all three sons attend school in Tai Po, and she hopes to minimise disruption to their lives, wishing to find a residence similar to Wang Fuk Court within the Tai Po district to rebuild a stable home. Yet she has still not found a suitable option for her family—the "Special Sales Scheme" sales brochure and detailed price list will only be released on 20 August, and the sheer volume of information cannot possibly be digested in such a short time; the new estate on Pok Yin Road West has poor transport access and will not be completed until 2030; if she were to purchase a second-hand HOS flat in Tai Po, she and her sons may not be able to bear the spectre of another major renovation; as for taking the compensation into the private property market, she still has an outstanding mortgage that cannot be ported, which she simply cannot afford, and it would be difficult to find suitable accommodation for a family of six.

All three options have limitations. Mrs Au said helplessly: "They only gave me all the options to consider at the very last minute—I don't have enough time to think, and I'm not confident I can pick a suitable option for my family. I'm not physically or mentally ready to sign this意向書." "It's not a matter of whether I want to or will consider it—it's that I really cannot decide... I cannot take this major decision for my family lightly."

Facing the risks: worries and disappointment

Over the past few days, various parties have repeatedly reminded owners to heed the 31 August deadline—the Wang Fuk Court title acquisition company earlier sent a letter stating that failing to return the意向書 by the deadline would be deemed as giving up participation in the long-term housing arrangement scheme; Deputy Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Chan Wai-lun also spoke up, saying the deadline was a "serious timetable" and would not be extended, and that legislation to resume the titles would be considered, with the outcome expected to be "significantly inferior" to the government's acquisition price.

Worried about being unable to withstand the mental pressure and breaking down

Mrs Au understands the government needs to set a deadline to move things forward, but as a disaster victim, she pointed out that while the government often says "people first," it also states that "once the decision is made, there's no turning back"—this stance has left her both heartbroken and disappointed. She does not shy away from expressing the risks she worries about having to bear, and indeed feels enormous pressure, but at this stage "I really cannot force myself to make this decision," "I'm very afraid of making the wrong decision, and I'm also very afraid I won't be able to withstand the mental pressure and break down."

Mrs Au had also considered returning the意向書 first, but she said that after the 30 June deadline, neighbours had reported that only after signing did they learn the terms included having to give up items inside the unit, and not being allowed to photocopy the sale and purchase agreement, making her worry about facing unacceptable terms.

Mrs Au reiterated that since the government announced the acquisition, she and her husband have been monitoring flat prices at various Tai Po estates, and had enquired with the explanation team about matters such as estate insurance and maintenance, but never received a reply; as the deadline approaches, the government and Hip Hing have been releasing information piecemeal, "as an owner, within such a short time, I am not physically or mentally ready to make this major decision."

Hoping government extends deadline, waiting for investigation report before selling

Although the government has made clear it will not extend the deadline, Mrs Au still hopes the government can put itself in disaster victims' shoes, understand that this matter is "a lifelong shadow," truly "put people first," and provide flexibility and room according to residents' different needs, extending the deadline so they have sufficient time to consider carefully and make important long-term decisions for their families that they will not regret.

She has always believed that, in principle, the title should only be sold after the investigation report is released and the cause and responsibility of the fire are clarified; she also finds it hard to accept that a charitable fund is being used to acquire the title. However, the independent committee has been granted an extension, and the report is not expected to be completed until late October.

"As a resident, what I really cannot let go of is the hope for a sequence of priorities—let me first understand what actually happened at Wang Fuk, why we suffered this misfortune, then tell me what choices I have, that I have to move forward, that I cannot return to Wang Fuk. I feel that with this sequence, as a resident, selling a place I love so much would feel more comfortable, and easier to accept."

"Not being able to wait for the independent investigation report before selling is, for me, a regret."

Despite the reluctance, still must build a new home

The government recently announced that 94.7% of owners have returned the意向書, leaving only about a hundred households who have not. Mrs Au said these numbers mean nothing to her, because whether to sell the title is a decision based on family needs, "it's not a game of minority服从多数." She also frankly said she cannot predict what will happen after 31 August: "If they really insist on acting according to legal principles, rather than the 'putting people first' they talked about, I have no choice—I will have to accept it reluctantly, and see how things develop afterwards."

Regarding Chan Wai-lun's remark that some owners had not returned the意向書 because they were unhappy with the acquisition price, Mrs Au said that was not her thinking, and stressed that she is not trying to be at odds with the government. She has always believed that the most responsible decision for her family is to see the road ahead clearly before deciding. If a suitable option is found, "actually I'm very willing to sign this意向書."

In previous interviews, she has repeatedly spoken of her affection for Wang Fuk Court as a place and the bonds among neighbours. Mrs Au frankly said she knows full well that nothing can be reversed, and selling the title is the only option, "whether I like it or not, it's my only option." Letting go of Wang Fuk, leaving Wang Fuk is an inevitable fact, and a decision forced by circumstances: "Even with a thousand reluctances, one must move forward, rebuild a new life... some things, one really must look ahead, some things, one must learn to accept."

"Home is where the people are"—this is what she often tells her three sons after the disaster. "I hope that even though neighbours are full of reluctance about Wang Fuk, they can all let go of Wang Fuk, move forward, and begin their own new lives."
